summary: Defines a common format, iCalendar, for openly exchanging calendaring and scheduling information across the Internet. It is the format behind many calendar files and invitations. It is a proposed standard that was replaced by RFC 5545.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a shared way to write down events, so that your phone, your computer and your friend's calendar can all understand the same invitation.

questions: what is the ics file format
how do calendar programs exchange events
how does icalendar line folding work
subtitle: The original text format for calendar events, to-dos and free/busy data that calendar programs swap as .ics files and invitations.

tldr.problem: Calendar programs from different vendors had no common format for exchanging events, to-dos, journal entries and free/busy information.
tldr.mechanism: iCalendar is a line-based text format of properties grouped into components such as VEVENT and VTODO, registered as the MIME type text/calendar and defined with a formal ABNF grammar.
tldr.outcome: It was a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 5545, which now defines iCalendar.

today: RFC 2445 was obsoleted by RFC 5545, which is the current definition of iCalendar.

sections.title: What iCalendar Is For
sections.content:
RFC 2445 defines the iCalendar data format for representing and exchanging calendaring and scheduling information such as events, to-dos, journal entries and free/busy information. It is intended for use as a MIME content type, but the RFC says it is not limited to that, and mentions transports such as the clipboard and infrared.

The format is only the core object. The RFC points to the iTIP interoperability protocol for scheduling operations such as requesting, replying to, modifying and canceling meetings, and to iMIP for an email binding. A formal ABNF grammar is the definitive reference when the prose is ambiguous.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone writes down their events in the same style, like all using the same kind of invitation card, so everyone can read them.

sections.title: Content Lines and Folding
sections.content:
An iCalendar object is plain text made of content lines ended by CRLF. Each has the shape name *(;param) : value. Names of properties, parameters and enumerated values are case-insensitive. Other values are case-sensitive unless stated otherwise.

Lines SHOULD NOT be longer than 75 octets. A longer line is folded by inserting a CRLF followed by one space or tab. A parser MUST first unfold such lines by removing that CRLF and the white space after it. Names starting with X- are reserved for experimental use.
sections.plainLanguage: Each fact goes on its own line. If a line gets too long, you can break it and start the next piece with a space, like a sentence wrapped onto the next line.

sections.title: Components and Properties
sections.content:
An iCalendar object has calendar properties and one or more calendar components, each wrapped in BEGIN: and END: lines. It MUST include the PRODID and VERSION properties and at least one component. Most often it holds a single VEVENT, VTODO or VJOURNAL.

The components are VEVENT (a scheduled amount of time), VTODO, VJOURNAL, VFREEBUSY, VTIMEZONE and VALARM. Component properties include DTSTART, DTEND, SUMMARY, UID, ORGANIZER and ATTENDEE. A VEVENT uses either DTEND or DURATION, but never both.

An alarm (VALARM) needs an ACTION and a TRIGGER. The alarm types in the grammar are audio, display, email and procedure.
sections.plainLanguage: An event is like a small form with labeled blanks: what, when, where and who is coming. A calendar file is a stack of such forms.

sections.title: Dates, Times and Repeats
sections.content:
A DATE-TIME value is a date, the letter T and a time, based on ISO 8601. It comes in three forms: local time with no zone ("floating"), UTC time, and local time with a TZID reference. Adding a UTC offset directly, as in 19980119T230000-0800, MUST NOT be used.

A floating time such as 19980118T230000 is read in whatever zone the attendee is in, so two attendees may meet at different real times. A fixed time needs UTC or a time zone reference. Time zones are described by VTIMEZONE components.

Repeating items use the RECUR type, with a FREQ from SECONDLY to YEARLY and optional parts such as INTERVAL, BYDAY and WKST. UNTIL and COUNT must not appear together.
sections.plainLanguage: A time written without a place means the same clock time for everyone, wherever they are. To pin it down to one moment you must say which time zone you mean.

sections.title: Security and Registration
sections.content:
The RFC registers the MIME type text/calendar, with optional parameters charset, method, component and optinfo. The file extension ics marks a file of calendaring data and ifb a file of free or busy time.

The security section names three concerns. Spoofing: only the Organizer should change or cancel an event, and only an Attendee should update their own ATTENDEE parameters, but someone else could forge such an object. Procedural alarms: a PROCEDURE alarm can carry an executable attachment and is open to malicious attack. Attachments: objects can reference URLs that point to programmable resources.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone could send a fake invitation or change someone else's event. And an alarm that runs a program could be used to sneak in something harmful.
